title: Employee and manager
prompt: Show each employee's name as employee and their manager's name as manager. Replace the ___.
hints: Match the manager's id with the employee's manager_id.

cases.name: Different data
cases.setupSql: DELETE FROM employees; DELETE FROM departments; INSERT INTO departments VALUES (5, 'Design'), (6, 'Finance'), (7, 'Ops'); INSERT INTO employees VALUES (11, 'Ivy', 5, NULL, 90000, '2019-02-01', 900, 'ivy@acme.test'), (12, 'Jon', 5, 11, 70000, '2020-06-15', NULL, NULL), (13, 'Kim', 6, 11, 70000, '2023-03-03', 300, 'kim@acme.test'), (14, 'Leo', NULL, 77, 30000, '2024-08-20', NULL, 'leo@acme.test'), (15, 'Mia', 6, 13, 55000, '2022-12-31', 0, 'mia@acme.test');

solutions: SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id;

wrongSolutions.sql: SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.id = m.manager_id;
SELECT e.name AS employee, e.name AS manager FROM employees e;

title: Who invited whom
prompt: Show each username as invited, and the username of the user who invited them as invited_by.
hints: referrer_id points to another user's id.
solutions: SELECT u.username AS invited, r.username AS invited_by FROM users u JOIN users r ON r.id = u.referrer_id;

wrongSolutions.sql: SELECT u.username AS invited, r.username AS invited_by FROM users u JOIN users r ON u.id = r.referrer_id;
SELECT u.username AS invited, u.referrer_id AS invited_by FROM users u;
wrongSolutions.why: Shows an id, not a name

title: Warmer than yesterday
prompt: Show the city and reading_date of readings warmer than the same city's reading on the previous calendar day.
hints: Join on city and on the date minus one day.
solutions: SELECT t.city, t.reading_date FROM readings t JOIN readings y ON y.city = t.city AND y.reading_date = date(t.reading_date, '-1 day') WHERE t.temp_c > y.temp_c;

wrongSolutions.sql: SELECT t.city, t.reading_date FROM readings t JOIN readings y ON y.city = t.city AND y.id = t.id - 1 WHERE t.temp_c > y.temp_c;
wrongSolutions.why: The previous row isn't always the previous day

wrongSolutions.sql: SELECT t.city, t.reading_date FROM readings t JOIN readings y ON y.reading_date = date(t.reading_date, '-1 day') WHERE t.temp_c > y.temp_c;

title: Pairs on the same salary
prompt: Find pairs of different employees with the same salary. Show name1 and name2, listing each pair once, with the lower id first.
hints: Using e.id < o.id removes reversed pairs and self-pairs.

cases.name: Different data
cases.setupSql: DELETE FROM employees; DELETE FROM departments; INSERT INTO departments VALUES (5, 'Design'), (6, 'Finance'), (7, 'Ops'); INSERT INTO employees VALUES (11, 'Ivy', 5, NULL, 90000, '2019-02-01', 900, 'ivy@acme.test'), (12, 'Jon', 5, 11, 70000, '2020-06-15', NULL, NULL), (13, 'Kim', 6, 11, 70000, '2023-03-03', 300, 'kim@acme.test'), (14, 'Leo', NULL, 77, 30000, '2024-08-20', NULL, 'leo@acme.test'), (15, 'Mia', 6, 13, 55000, '2022-12-31', 0, 'mia@acme.test');

solutions: SELECT e.name AS name1, o.name AS name2 FROM employees e JOIN employees o ON e.salary = o.salary AND e.id < o.id;

wrongSolutions.sql: SELECT e.name AS name1, o.name AS name2 FROM employees e JOIN employees o ON e.salary = o.salary;
SELECT e.name AS name1, o.name AS name2 FROM employees e JOIN employees o ON e.salary = o.salary AND e.id <> o.id;

title: Earning more than their manager
prompt: Show the name of employees who earn more than their manager.
hints: Compare the two copies in WHERE.

cases.name: Different data
cases.setupSql: DELETE FROM employees; DELETE FROM departments; INSERT INTO departments VALUES (5, 'Design'), (6, 'Finance'), (7, 'Ops'); INSERT INTO employees VALUES (11, 'Ivy', 5, NULL, 90000, '2019-02-01', 900, 'ivy@acme.test'), (12, 'Jon', 5, 11, 70000, '2020-06-15', NULL, NULL), (13, 'Kim', 6, 11, 70000, '2023-03-03', 300, 'kim@acme.test'), (14, 'Leo', NULL, 77, 30000, '2024-08-20', NULL, 'leo@acme.test'), (15, 'Mia', 6, 13, 55000, '2022-12-31', 0, 'mia@acme.test'); UPDATE employees SET salary = 95000 WHERE id = 15; UPDATE employees SET salary = 60000 WHERE id = 13;

solutions: SELECT e.name FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id WHERE e.salary > m.salary;

wrongSolutions.sql: SELECT e.name FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id WHERE e.salary < m.salary;
SELECT m.name FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id WHERE e.salary > m.salary;

title: Team sizes
prompt: Show each manager's name as manager, how many people report to them as reports, and the average salary of those reports as avg_salary, rounded to a whole number, sorted by manager.

cases.name: Different data
cases.setupSql: DELETE FROM employees; DELETE FROM departments; INSERT INTO departments VALUES (5, 'Design'), (6, 'Finance'), (7, 'Ops'); INSERT INTO employees VALUES (11, 'Ivy', 5, NULL, 90000, '2019-02-01', 900, 'ivy@acme.test'), (12, 'Jon', 5, 11, 70000, '2020-06-15', NULL, NULL), (13, 'Kim', 6, 11, 70000, '2023-03-03', 300, 'kim@acme.test'), (14, 'Leo', NULL, 77, 30000, '2024-08-20', NULL, 'leo@acme.test'), (15, 'Mia', 6, 13, 55000, '2022-12-31', 0, 'mia@acme.test'); UPDATE employees SET salary = 70001 WHERE id = 12;

solutions: SELECT m.name AS manager, COUNT(*) AS reports, ROUND(AVG(e.salary)) AS avg_salary FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id GROUP BY m.id, m.name ORDER BY manager;

wrongSolutions.sql: SELECT m.name AS manager, COUNT(*) AS reports, AVG(e.salary) AS avg_salary FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id GROUP BY m.id, m.name ORDER BY manager;
SELECT e.name AS manager, COUNT(*) AS reports, ROUND(AVG(e.salary)) AS avg_salary FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id GROUP BY e.id, e.name ORDER BY manager;
